title: How to localize training and product videos without losing your mind
summary: How to translate a video without re-recording it: reuse one source recording, build a translation glossary, and turn each new language into a review pass.
body_markdown:
Your product ships in one language but your users might hail from various parts of the world. A support lead in São Paulo, a new hire in Osaka, and a customer in Munich all need the same onboarding walkthrough, and right now someone in marketing is booking a studio to record it three more times.[Translating a video](https://www.clueso.io/tools/video-translator) sounds like a subtitle problem until you try it, and then it becomes a voiceover problem, a screenshot problem, and a terminology problem at the same time.


Most teams solve this the expensive way. They re-record the whole walkthrough per language, or they hand a video to an agency and wait two weeks for a version where the product name got translated into something that means nothing to your users. There's a faster path, and it starts with treating your source recording as an asset you reuse rather than a take you redo.


## What does it actually take to translate a video?


To translate a video, you replace its spoken audio and on-screen text with a target language: transcribe the original, translate the script, generate a new voiceover, then update captions, interface labels, and screenshots to match. At scale, the trick is reusing one source recording across every language instead of re-recording it each time.


That last part is where teams either save weeks or lose them. A single English walkthrough carries everything a Spanish, French, or Japanese version needs — the pacing, the on-screen actions, the structure. What changes is the language layer on top, and that layer can be produced and reviewed far faster than a fresh recording.


## Why re-recording is the wrong default


Re-recording feels safe because you control every frame, but it doesn't scale past two or three languages. Every time your product UI changes, you're back in the studio for all of them, and you're depending on a fluent speaker being available for each one. The cost isn't only the recording session. It's the scheduling, the retakes, and the drift between versions that creeps in when the English walkthrough gets updated and the German one doesn't.


Consider a team maintaining a 12-video onboarding series in six languages. Re-recording means 72 recording sessions to keep in sync, and a single UI change to one feature can invalidate a chunk of all six. Translate from a single source instead, and that same UI change means updating one recording and re-running the language layer.


> That's not hypothetical: over the past year, Clueso customers have localized videos into 38 languages this way, reusing a single source recording rather than re-shooting each one per language.

## How do you build a translation glossary?


A[translation glossary](https://www.clueso.io/features/translation-glossary) is a shared list of terms with a rule for each one: translate it, don't translate it, or render it a specific way. It's the difference between your product name staying intact and an automatic translator turning "Inbox Zero" into a phrase your German users have never heard. Build it once at the account level, and every video you translate inherits it.


Start with three categories. Do-not-translate terms cover product names, feature names, and branded UI labels that should read identically in every language. Preferred renderings cover words that do get translated but have a house choice — how you say "dashboard," "workspace," or "report" when the language offers several options. Dialect and formality rules cover the choices that change meaning, like Latin American versus European Spanish, or the level of politeness a Japanese voiceover should use with an enterprise audience.


The glossary also needs pronunciation guidance for AI voiceover. A term that reads correctly on screen can still be spoken wrong, so note how product names should sound out loud, especially acronyms and invented words. Keep the glossary in one place, version it, and treat it as the source of truth every translated video pulls from.


## When should you tune AI translation per language?


[AI video translation](https://www.clueso.io/blog/ai-video-translation) is not evenly good across languages, and pretending it is will burn you on your first Japanese release. For European languages that share structure and a lot of vocabulary with English, the first pass is usually close enough that a reviewer is polishing rather than rewriting. For languages with different word order, honorifics, or scripts, the model needs more guidance and the output needs a real human check before it ships.


The practical move is to set a review level per language and encode the recurring fixes as glossary rules and examples. If your Japanese reviewer keeps correcting the same formality choice, that's a rule, not a one-off edit. Here's a rough starting map for how much attention each group tends to need.


Language group Typical first-pass quality What still needs a human Glossary rules that matter most


Spanish, French, Portuguese, German High — light polish Regional word choice, tone Dialect (LatAm vs. European), preferred renderings


Italian, Dutch, Polish Good — moderate review Idiom, sentence flow Do-not-translate terms, formality


Japanese, Korean Variable — heavy review Honorifics, word order, naturalness Formality level, pronunciation, do-not-translate terms


Arabic, Hebrew Variable — heavy review Right-to-left layout, dialect On-screen text direction, dialect


Treat this as a default you adjust with your own reviewers' feedback. The point is to decide the review level before you translate, so a hard language doesn't get the same rushed pass as an easy one.

## What about on-screen text and screenshots?


This is the part teams forget until a reviewer flags it. If your product interface is localized, a Spanish voiceover playing over English screenshots looks broken, and it undercuts the trust the video is supposed to build. Translating the audio is only half the job when the visuals are carrying the actual steps.


You have two options, and which one you pick depends on how localized your product is. If the UI is translated, switch your product to the target locale and re-capture the screen for each language, so the clicks the viewer sees match the clicks they'll make. If the UI is English-only, keep the source screenshots and rely on translated captions and voiceover to carry the meaning. Either way, on-screen labels you add yourself — callouts, titles, annotations — should pull from the same glossary as the voiceover so a term isn't translated one way in the audio and another way on screen.

## A workflow you can run this week


Start by recording the source walkthrough once, in your strongest language, and lock it. Build or update your glossary with the product names, preferred renderings, and dialect rules for the languages you're targeting. Then generate the language layer — translated script, AI voiceover, and[captions](https://www.clueso.io/features/video-captions) — for each language, review against the glossary, and re-capture screenshots for any locale where the UI is translated.

For teams without a dedicated video crew, that's the difference between shipping six languages and shipping one. ## Frequently asked questions


### How do you translate a video without re-recording it?


Keep the original screen recording as your visual source and replace only the language layer. Transcribe the audio, translate the script using your glossary, generate an AI voiceover in the target language, and update captions. You re-record nothing unless the product UI itself is localized and needs fresh screenshots.


### Is AI translation accurate enough for training videos?


For European languages —[English to Spanish](https://www.clueso.io/tools/translate-english-to-spanish) , for instance — it's usually strong enough that a reviewer polishes rather than rewrites. For languages like Japanese, Korean, and Arabic, treat the first pass as a draft and budget for human review. A glossary with per-language rules and examples closes most of the recurring gaps.


### Why does a translation glossary matter so much?


Without one, an automatic translator will translate your product and feature names, and different videos will render the same term differently. An account-wide glossary defines do-not-translate terms, preferred renderings, dialect rules, and pronunciation, so every translated video stays consistent and on-brand.


### How do you handle on-screen text and screenshots when translating?


If your product UI is localized, switch the product to the target language and re-capture the screen so the visuals match the voiceover. If the UI is English-only, keep the original screenshots and let translated captions and voiceover carry the steps. Pull any callouts or titles you add from the same glossary as the audio.


Pick one onboarding video, build the glossary for your top three languages, and translate that single video end to end this week. Once the glossary exists and the workflow is proven on one video, the fourth and fifth languages cost you a review pass, not another studio booking.
